title: Hacking enlightenment: can ultrasound help you transcend reality?
description: Can technology improve the way we meditate? At the University of Arizona, Dr Jay Sanguinetti and master meditator Shinzen Young are using ultrasound to improve our ability to achieve mindfulness – as well as enhance our cognition and wellbeing. Subscribe to The Guardian on YouTube ► http://bit.ly/subscribegdn  They believe it could revolutionise the way we treat those with depression and trauma. But as investors from Silicon Valley become interested in the technology, the pair are fighting to make sure the device is used in the right way and for the right reasons.  The Guardian publishes independent journalism, made possible by supporters. Contribute to The Guardian today ► https://bit.ly/3biVfwh  Sign up to the Guardian's free new daily newsletter, First Edition ► http://theguardian.com/first-edition  Website ► https://www.theguardian.com Facebook ► https://www.facebook.com/theguardian Twitter ► https://twitter.com/guardian Instagram ► https://www.instagram.com/guardian  The Guardian on YouTube:  Guardian News ► https://bit.ly/guardiannewssubs Guardian Australia ► https://bit.ly/guardianaussubs Guardian Football ► https://bit.ly/gdnfootballsubs Guardian Sport ► https://bit.ly/gdnsportsubs Guardian Live ► https://bit.ly/guardianlivesubs  #Enlightenment #Meditation #SiliconValley #Depression #MentalHealth

asr.full_text: When I was at the Society for Neuroscience meeting I heard the Dalai Lama say that if neuroscientists could create an intervention to give him the effects of meditation without meditating he would be the first one to sign up. Ultrasound might be it. If you pardon my French we are scared shitless of this technology. We're just at the very beginning of unlocking this immense technological and scientific power. As I create technology that helps you become happier, does that reduce your ability to make good decisions? How do we define good decisions? I have a little delay. It's all good, though. And I'll just be there around unit. That was Shenzhen. He's the lab co-director, Shenzunish. That was Shinzen. He's the lab co-director, Shinzen Young. He is very special. His real name is Steve Young, so he doesn't look like what you might expect Shinzen to look like. He became Shinzen because he'd became ordained as a Buddhist monk in Japan in the 1970s, I believe. Here's toilet reading. Would be the Feynman Lectures on Physics. On top of that, Shenzhen is also a science geek, and so he's this trifecta in this field. I've seen him cry literally describing mathematical theorems. So, I met Shenzhen in graduate school, and I really wanted to know what can we know about brain activity that would explain to us how consciousness emerges? Jay and I had a relationship that built over several years, so I started to teach him some of our techniques, and we started to talk about how ultrasonic neuromodulation would be relevant to these techniques. And then, there was a point at which it's like, let's do ultrasound and mindfulness. This is where I used to come meditate, because you get a bit of shade. We can change the way the brain functions for positive effects in terms of a broad spectrum of human happiness goals. Alright. Ready to go? Yeah. How you doing? Let's do it. Shenzhen was also the first subject for trying to combine non-invasive brain stimulation and meditation practice. So, we're going to do Day 3 of the protocol that we've been doing. What we're targeting with ultrasound is quieting a brain network that is active in all of us. And when it's active it's often responsible for some negative self-focused thought and causes people to distress. So, by targeting the posterior cingulate cortex, we seem to be disrupting the activity of that network, giving it just a little less ability to self-organize again. People will say in our studies, I still had those thoughts but I wasn't angry about them. I was able to observe my thoughts. Because the ultrasound is so highly focused, we have to set the target for each individual subject, so it seems like meditation targets that specific brain area, we're trying to boost the effect of meditation by making it happen a little bit faster. Everything is so vivid that it's a kind of nothing. That's why he just laughed, it's like, very big and very small, very rich and very thin, exactly the same time. What kind of power do you see? That power is what I'm seeing. That power is how I am. How do you see the world? I can see the land of the past. I can see your spirit. I can see what I've lost, I can see your joy. You do what you want with that power. I can see why it takes so long to grow. I can see where we are with that power. I can see your power. I can feel you come to me from above. I can see your love for me. I am your God... I am your light. You can see, I love to be surprised. I was really scared and angry...a lot. And I was dealing with a lot of trauma. We're starting to actually have a chance to treat the deep conditions that are leading to a lot of the issues that we're worried about. Depression, anxiety, all of those realize I was holding that tension. It's like releasing a muscle that you've been holding tight for your whole life. Ultrasound is not the first wave that we've injected from outside the skull into people to try to have some beneficial effects. And if we go way back in the 40s and 50s, people delivered electroshock. That was seen as, by many, inhumane. Yeah, I think the RA came in and she said, it's been five minutes. Do you want to do a little bit more? I was like, absolutely. Yes, please. I was able to sink into equanimity very quickly. So if you have depression, if you have chronic pain, if you're suffering from addiction, mindfulness is not really something that you want to do. You don't want to sit with yourself for, you know, even 30 seconds, let alone 30 minutes. This removes the barriers to entry and makes it more rewarding upfront so that you can do the work. We hope that this technology will have huge positive benefits in terms of human happiness, reduction of suffering, elevation of fulfillment, self-understanding, positive behavior change, and ultimately a call to service is where we want this technology to culminate. My experience in the Bay Area didn't work out quite as I had planned. The Bay Area is all about growing technology exponentially, finding a unicorn and making that a billion dollar company and then growing it from there. I realized that the culture there wasn't quite what I needed to build this... ...in a safe, slow, scientific, and kind of boring way. I don't have anything inherently wrong with money... ...but I understand it's a corrupting influence. That may set you up... ...for creating a relatively dangerous brain stimulation system. We might not be right at this point to just create... ...something that you sell on Amazon and tell people to use it every day. We just don't know if that's safe. And as a scientist, that's what I have to say. I hope we know what we're doing along the way, and i hope that we engage it with mindfulness and being careful and thoughtful, and not just doing things because we can There might be doses and locations in the brain that you can definitely have a holy cow effect right whoa give me that one again. That's not our goal to target those, that it's not to say people won't figure that out, but this shouldn't be a high it should be a therapeutic tool. This technology scares me, and the future without a radical improvement really scares me. the future without a radical improvement really scares me a lot, lot more. So that's why we've got to Democratize Enlightenment.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it is framed as a Guardian documentary inquiry into whether ultrasound can affect meditation and mindfulness, featuring researchers and a meditation teacher. The content discusses a proposed brain target, head-mounted equipment, and safety limitations for consumer use, rather than presenting a risky money-making or credential-collection offer. The closing subscribe and support prompts are ordinary publisher engagement.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary subject is educational and operational discussion of a technology and research procedure: the source explains targeting a brain network with ultrasound, describes an attempt to enhance meditation, and frames the equipment as a research or therapeutic tool rather than an earning or investment mechanism.

evidence.observation: The speaker explains the proposed neurological target of the ultrasound procedure.
evidence.quote: What we're targeting with ultrasound is quieting a brain network that is active in all of us.

evidence.observation: The speaker describes the intended relationship between ultrasound and meditation practice.
evidence.quote: we're trying to boost the effect of meditation by making it happen a little bit faster

evidence.observation: The speaker expresses uncertainty about consumer deployment and safety.
evidence.quote: We might not be right at this point to just create... ...something that you sell on Amazon and tell people to use it every day. We just don't know if that's safe.

evidence.observation: A person is shown receiving a head-mounted device while another person adjusts equipment on their head.
An illustrated brain diagram visibly identifies the posterior cingulate cortex.
